slides.say: a is an odd positive number, and b is an even positive number. Which of the following expressions is not necessarily an integer?

So every choice is over eight, and eight is three twos. Three choices always have enough twos on top, and one doesn't. [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, counting the twos, and then plugging in the smallest numbers.
[short pause] Let's count the twos. b is even, so b is two k.
Choice number one, b cubed is two k, cubed, eight k cubed. The whole eight is there, always whole. Out.
Choice number two. a is odd, so a plus one and a plus three are two consecutive even numbers, and they always divide by eight. Out.
at: a plus one and a plus three

slides.say: Choice number three. Open both squares. The two a b terms cancel, and two a squared plus two b squared, minus two a squared, leaves two b squared. That's two times four k squared, eight k squared. Out.

Choice number four, a times b squared. b squared is four k squared, two twos, and a is odd, no twos at all. Only two twos, and eight needs three. A third two can come from k by luck, but not necessarily. Choice number four is our answer.
at: Choice number four is our answer

slides.say: Let's see it in numbers. a is one and b is two, four over eight is a half. But a is one and b is four, sixteen over eight is two. Whole by luck.
at: a is one and b is two

slides.say: [pause] Now let's try plugging in. Which numbers? The smallest, a is one and b is two, so no extra two sneaks in.
Choice number one, two cubed is eight, times three is twenty-four, over eight is three. Choice number two, two times four is eight, over eight is one.
Choice number three, nine plus one minus two is eight, over eight is one. Choice number four, one times four is four, over eight is a half. Not whole, so choice number four.
at: Not whole, so choice number four

slides.say: And see why the smallest. With b four, choice number four gives sixteen over eight, two, and it would hide the answer. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
